clinicalPearls: A distinct subset of gastrointestinal stromal tumours lacking KIT and PDGFRA mutations ('wild-type') and defined by loss of SDHB immunostaining.
Almost always gastric, typically multifocal and multinodular with a plexiform architecture and epithelioid or mixed cytology.
Shows a predilection for children, adolescents and young adults, with a female predominance, and was historically termed the 'paediatric GIST'.
May metastasise to lymph nodes, which is exceptional for conventional GIST, yet often follows an indolent course even in the presence of metastases.
Occurs sporadically, within the Carney triad (GIST, paraganglioma, pulmonary chondroma) and within the Carney–Stratakis dyad (GIST plus paraganglioma).
Germline SDHA/B/C/D variants underlie Carney–Stratakis and many apparently sporadic cases, whereas the Carney triad is usually driven by epigenetic SDHC promoter hypermethylation.
Responds poorly to imatinib because there is no KIT or PDGFRA target, so management centres on surgery with careful long-term follow-up.
Loss of SDHA staining in addition to SDHB specifically points to an underlying SDHA mutation.
reference.pathophysiology: These tumours arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal but, unlike conventional gastrointestinal stromal tumours, are not driven by activating KIT or PDGFRA mutations. Instead they show deficiency of the succinate dehydrogenase complex, arising through germline SDHA/B/C/D mutation, epigenetic silencing of SDHC by promoter hypermethylation, or biallelic somatic events. Whichever mechanism operates, the complex is destabilised and SDHB protein is lost on immunohistochemistry. Resulting succinate accumulation inhibits alpha-ketoglutarate–dependent dioxygenases, stabilises hypoxia-inducible factors and produces a pseudohypoxic, pro-angiogenic and globally hypermethylated state that drives tumourigenesis independent of receptor tyrosine kinase signalling. This distinct biology underlies the gastric multifocality, the propensity for nodal spread and the relative resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitors that characterise the group.
additionalDifferentials: Other Carney triad components such as paraganglioma or pulmonary chondroma
additionalInvestigations: SDHB immunohistochemistry, with SDHA staining, on tumour tissue
KIT and PDGFRA mutation analysis to confirm wild-type status
Germline SDHx genetic testing with referral to clinical genetics
Endoscopy with endoscopic ultrasound and biopsy for gastric lesions
Cross-sectional staging imaging of the abdomen and pelvis with assessment for paraganglioma
Plasma or urinary metanephrines to screen for an associated paraganglioma or phaeochromocytoma
Chest imaging for pulmonary chondroma when the Carney triad is suspected
redFlags: Gastrointestinal haemorrhage or symptomatic anaemia from an ulcerated gastric tumour
Multifocal gastric masses with regional lymphadenopathy in a young patient
Concurrent catecholamine symptoms suggesting an associated paraganglioma
Rapid tumour growth or new hepatic metastases indicating disease progression
reference.prognosis: SDH-deficient GIST typically behaves indolently, and patients may survive for many years even with nodal or hepatic metastases, although disease is often persistent and recurrent. Complete surgical resection is the mainstay because response to tyrosine kinase inhibitors is limited, so prolonged surveillance is essential.
pitfalls: Applying conventional GIST risk-stratification based on size and mitotic count, which does not reliably predict behaviour in SDH-deficient tumours.
Prescribing imatinib as for typical GIST, when SDH-deficient tumours are largely unresponsive.
Failing to test for germline SDHx variants and to screen for paraganglioma, phaeochromocytoma and pulmonary chondroma.
Interpreting nodal metastasis as evidence of an aggressive conventional sarcoma and over-treating accordingly.
